extracted.intended_audience: general public, journalists, policymakers, and students researching UK press regulation and public inquiries
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style encyclopedic overview of the Leveson Inquiry (2011–12) covering its terms of reference, proceedings, findings and recommendations about press regulation in the UK. Useful for readers seeking a concise summary of the inquiry's scope, process and key proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Part 1 terms of reference (scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: "the culture, practices and ethics of the press, including contacts between the press and politicians and the press and the police; it is to consider the extent to which the current regulatory regime has failed and whether there has been a failure to act upon any previous warnings about media misconduct."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part 1 is framed to examine broad ethical and cultural issues in press behaviour, relationships with politicians and police, and systemic regulatory failures; it should therefore solicit evidence addressing culture, practices, ethics, and regulatory adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Part 2 terms of reference (scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: "the extent of unlawful or improper conduct within News International, other media organisations or other organisations. It will also consider the extent to which any relevant police force investigated allegations relating to News International, and whether the police received corrupt payments or were otherwise complicit in misconduct."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part 2 was intended to investigate alleged unlawful conduct and the adequacy/integrity of police investigations; it was to follow Part 1 but was delayed and later shelved because of ongoing criminal investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of existing regulator (PCC adequacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leveson found that the existing Press Complaints Commission was not sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should consider whether an existing self-regulatory body can meet the standards of independence, sanctions and public confidence required to protect victims and uphold media standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation: new independent regulatory body
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommend a new independent body to replace the Press Complaints Commission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed body should be independent of the industry, able to command public and political confidence, and structured to address the deficiencies identified in the PCC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory sanctions and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: The new body would have a range of sanctions available to it, including fines and direction of the prominence of apologies and corrections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions should include both financial penalties and remedial directions (e.g., prominence of corrections/apologies) to ensure effective redress and deterrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary membership with incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Membership of the body would be voluntary, but incentivised by schemes such as a kitemark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than statutory compulsion, uptake should be encouraged via reputational signals (kitemarks) and other benefits that make participation advantageous to publishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquisitorial arbitration service for tort claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal for an inquisitorial arbitration service for handling tort claims such as libel and breach of privacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide an alternative dispute-resolution mechanism (inquisitorial arbitration) to resolve privacy/libel disputes efficiently and fairly, reducing reliance on adversarial court processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of exemplary damages to incentivise participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing exemplary damages to be awarded in cases brought against non-participants in the scheme, something not usually part of English law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a legal disincentive for non-participation by permitting exemplary damages in actions against publishers who choose not to join the regulator, thereby encouraging industry uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding characterisation as statutory regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Leveson rejected the characterisation of his proposal as 'statutory regulation of the press'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposals aim to preserve press freedom by avoiding direct statutory control, while still creating effective incentives and sanctions through a non-statutory but robust regime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations on data protection and ICO powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Leveson made recommendations regarding the Data Protection Act and the powers and duties of the Information Commissioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any reform should consider strengthening data-protection law and enforcement (ICO powers) as part of broader media-ethics and privacy protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for relations between press, police and politicians
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendations about conduct of relations between the press, the police, and politicians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance should address conflicts of interest, improper contacts, disclosure practices and safeguards to protect the integrity of policing and political processes in relation to media activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inquiry procedural design (modules, witnesses, core participants)
rubrics_metrics.description: The inquiry was run over three modules addressing (1) press and public, (2) press and police, (3) press and politicians; it called 337 witnesses and designated core participants such as media organisations, police and victims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A public inquiry into systemic media issues may be structured modularly to focus hearings on specific relationships, should allow witness testimony and statements, and provide core participant status to relevant organisations and victims to ensure representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling anonymous evidence and judicial review limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Associated Newspapers Ltd challenged a ruling on the admissibility of anonymous evidence; the presiding judges refused judicial review on grounds that anonymity requests should be dealt with by the chairman of the inquiry rather than the judiciary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedures should give the inquiry chair discretion over anonymity and sensitive evidence; courts may be reluctant to intervene while an inquiry manages such matters internally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay or suspension of inquiry modules pending criminal investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Part 2 would have been addressed later because of ongoing investigations by law enforcement; by 2015 it had been shelved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When criminal proceedings or police investigations are ongoing, inquiry components that could prejudice those processes may be delayed or modified to avoid interference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of funding and potential conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The Inquiry was funded through two Government departments and appointed a panel of advisers; reporting of social engagements (e.g., Leveson attending parties) led to scrutiny and calls for removal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public inquiries should disclose funding sources, panel membership and consider potential conflicts of interest or appearances of bias; perceived closeness between inquiry figures and stakeholders can undermine confidence and should be managed.
